speechtext:

In view of the very recent marine accident which has damaged a key railway bridge providing CN access to the port of Vancouver, in view of the potentially dire consequences for the port as a result of this accident, which may cut capacity by 15 per cent and cause millions of dollars in lost business, and in view of the backlog in grain shipments already causing congestion in the port, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43 I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an extremely urgent matter.
As the mandate of the government is that of a minority government, and as we could soon find ourselves in the midst of an election campaign; as all hon. members who have lived through an election know that campaigns are unduly long; as there is no permanent voters' list and as the Chief Electoral Officer has already submitted a study suggesting solutions to that problem, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster):

As I indicated earlier today, there will be no significant action with regard to Petro-Canada without the approval of Parliament. subsubtopic: GRAIN DELIVERIES FROM PORT OF VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to reply to this very important question, and I appreciate the motion under Standing Order 43 which was moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
I have been in touch with officials of the CNR and the Canadian Wheat Board, and as of this point in time the CNR has requested and received tenders for the repair of the bridge. I think the Canadian Wheat Board at this very moment is meeting and putting some contingency plans in place. It is the number one item on the agenda. Mr. Speaker, I will indicate to the hon. member again what is the intention of the government. The Yukon territorial government is a body of elected people who have the responsibility to look after the day to day affairs of the territory.
With regard to the commissioner, there were certain responsibilities which the commissioner had held previously which, under the terms of the Yukon Act, could be transferred to the elected representatives in the Yukon. The former commissioner felt that the move toward responsible government was coming too quickly. We do not believe that it was coming too quickly; in fact, we favour the elected people of the Yukon obtaining more responsibility.
What should also be stated clearly to the hon. member is that we have indicated that, in terms of provincial status, this is not a move toward provincial status in the sense that the Prime Minister clearly indicated during the election campaign that responsibility would be transferred to the Yukon and that after full consultation with the various groups, with a responsible government in place, the people of the Yukon would be asked for their opinion on whether or not provincial status was agreeable to them. That was the position of the government, and we have not changed it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reference to the comment made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker), can we have a clear and unequivocal confirmation or otherwise from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) that he takes his responsibility for making recommendations on these estimates to Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO STANDING COMMITTEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understood that the matter had been dealt with rather conclusively by the Chair on Friday. A parliamentarian of the standing of the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Andras) should know what that position is. The situation now, sir, is that before this House there stands a motion in my name to refer the estimates to the committees which were established by this House, by consent, last week. That motion is neither debatable nor amendable. 1 suggest we get on with dealing with the motion so that the committees can get to work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES TO STANDING COMMITTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Privy Council has referred to a procedural ruling made by Your Honour, which we accept. He has proposed that the estimates go to committee. We will deal with that motion when it is put to the House.

Let me tell my hon. friend, however, that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) will not be able to escape his political and parliamentary responsibilities in recommending to the House of Commons expenditures of over $1 billion. He will not get away in the House with the comment he made to the press, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen, to the effect that he was not going to recommend programs or figures that he had no hand in drawing up. If that is his attitude, he is going to have a tough time getting these estimates through the House.

Pursuant to Standing Order 59, the motion which has now been moved by the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) is properly before the House. The form of the motion is the rather standard one. Since these estimates have to be moved to various committees, which has been the practice of the House in the past, rather than using the time of the House to read the various estimates and votes and the particular committees to which he referred, a list has customarily been attached to that effect. Therefore, I would take it that the sense of the House is that the motion is in the usual form, and it is the intention of the House to deal with that aspect as though the list attached to the motion had been read with the motion.
The House has heard the terms of the motion. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for all those who were here on Friday during the last five minutes I dealt
October 15, 1979

with congratulations, and now I would like to go into the crux of my reply to the Speech from the Throne. I want to thank my leader and my party for giving me the opportunity to make my maiden speech in the House-it is an honour for the riding of Argenteuil that their representative be chosen for such an occasion.
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Argenteuil has been part of the history of Canada since the beginning of confederation, and judging by recent events, Argenteuil will be heard from even more this year at this time of crisis on national unity.
But furthermore, Mr. Speaker, this riding has lot to offer in terms of culture and economic development potential. The riding of Argenteuil is divided into five distinct areas: first, the Petite Nation where unemployment at times reaches the scandalous rate of 33 per cent; that is why, Mr. Speaker, I find the Speech from the Throne of the Progressive Conservatives very conservative in its measures to improve the unemployment situation. Then there are Lachute, Brownsburg and the surrounding areas which used to be the industrial nerve centre in Argenteuil and which are being eroded to the point of nearly disappearing. All sorts of corporations are leaving behind huge, unproductive and empty plants. In this regard also, Mr. Speaker, I deplore the lack of incentive given in the Speech from the Throne to small and medium business which in my riding is the only means of survival in the industrial sector.

The region of St. Adolphe, where nature is at its best throughout the year, has become a natural paradise for tourism all year long. It is so agreeable that both the leader of the national Liberals and the leader of the provincial Liberals has taken up residence in this beautiful sector of Argenteuil.
I was pleased to see in the Speech from the Throne that provision was made for a strategy to be developed, but I am amazed, Mr. Speaker, that at a stage where the provinces are concerned, we are only talking of strategy when we all know it is time for action. [DOT]
[ Translation]
Mirabel! Mirabel! I am pleading directly with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), Mr. Speaker. It is unthinkable that such a potentially rich area should be paralysed because of administrative bureaucracy. I am therefore asking the minister to involve himself directly in this matter so that a rapid transit system can be developed between Montreal and Mirabel which would benefit over a million people and would facilitate the development of this airport complex which is the gateway to North America. The economic expansion of Mirabel would also benefit the Oka and St. Placid region.
The Address-Mr. Gourd
Mr. Speaker, that is the brief overview of the situation in Argenteuil that I wanted to give the House. 1 am convinced that, the government willing, 1 will not have to quote what the hon. member for Chapleau said in this House on August 16, 1946. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), both in his press conference and here in this House, spoke of co-operation with all members of Parliament.
I wish to congratulate the government which is concerned with the fate of our cultural industries. Unfortunately I note, Mr. Speaker, that such concern is misdirected because it is centred on the accessory and ignores the essential. Who are, in the first place, our cultural producers? The authors. Now, those authors are barely protected under a single law already more than half a century old. Nowhere in the throne speech has the government shown that it is fully aware of that issue when throughout Canada the authors are loudly demanding to the Prime Minister himself that vigorous political action be undertaken.
What is hindering the settlement of the matter? First, an interdepartmental committee met without knowing exactly what it was going to do, because nobody assumed responsibility. Then, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) who is responsible for the administration of the Copyright Act is not concerned with the interests of the authors, since he is dealing with those who exploit the works of the authors and not with the authors themselves.
The solution, Mr. Speaker, is quite simple, and 1 fully agree with the many authors and artists who are begging the government to transfer immediately responsibility for that sector from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to the Department of the Secretary of State which is in a better position to undertake as soon as possible the most important review for safeguarding the Canadian culture, that is, of the Copyright Act.
Mr. Speaker, what the government is prepared to do for our Canadian artists seems to me to be too little and too late, and by breaking up Loto Canada it is missing an opportunity to support them since part of the revenues of that agency could have been used to subsidize our artists. Mr. Speaker, my slogan throughout the campaign was "Speak up, Argenteuil", and that is exactly what 1 intend to do in the face of this government which, from the start, seems at a loss to know what to do with its power and already shows indications of growing dullness.
1 wonder, Mr. Speaker, why this government of our Tory friends, who fiercely denounced the budget introduced by the former finance minister, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), has not found time in four months to produce any fresh ideas. Instead, it has raised interest rates once again to penalize the population and help the big and powerful friends of the Tories grow wealthier. True, 1 was about to forget the provision to help landlords, only to the detriment of tenants. These are the not so fresh ideas, Mr. Speaker. We

October 15, 1979
The Address-Mr. Binks
have in front of us a government of novices whose internal wranglings are paralysing the good administration of our country. Those super-ministers of pseudo super departments, who became super-salesmen, proved to us who they really were with the sale of Candu to Argentina, which once again, Mr. Speaker, will penalize the Canadian public.
I cannot refrain from saying a few words about the embassy case at a time when all nations are attempting to solve the problems faced by Israel and Egypt. Our government, Mr. Speaker, is taking up the whole matter again only for tiny political gains. Those are, Mr. Speaker, the views of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) on a strong and respected Canada. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I must say that, as the member for Argenteuil in the opposition, my intention is to observe carefully the sayings and doings of this administration and to look after the interests of my constituency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate you on your election as Speaker of the House of Commons. In the past you accomplished your historical duties in such a way that you added dignity and respect to the parliamentary process. I join other members in congratulating also the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I wish them much success in their careers in the House and in the service of the public.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today with what I can assure you is a great deal of trepidation but a heart full of pride. Like so many members of this House, and those that have gone before me, I have spent a lifetime in the shadow of the Peace Tower. From the nearest public school to these buildings, our teacher often brought us here to sit in the gallery. My grandfather photographed the great fire of February 1916, and sent photographs of it to the four corners of the world. My uncle welded the gargoyles just beneath the great clock on the Peace Tower itself.
When I was a young man, it was my privilege to work within the walls of this great building for two years as a library assistant in the Parliamentary Library. My wife was the private secretary to the leader of the CCF. She came to the library to borrow a book one day and, needless to say, my love for the Library and, indeed, for the whole institution of Parliament has never diminished. I still have the same faith in and awe for this House of Commons as I did as a schoolboy in the gallery.
[ Translation]
When Mr. Arthur Meighen was asked the secret of his rapid rise in the House of Commons, he would simply reply, "The Parliamentary Library."
[ English]
Senator Gratton O'Leary once wrote that if he were asked by a young member of Parliament for his advice, he would say

unhesitatingly to him, "Study, listen and wear a path to the Parliamentary Library, and reverence always the House of Commons". So for many years I have watched the various Parliaments, our great leaders and the many hundred worthy members who have gone before.
On this auspicious occasion, I say it is an honour for me to represent the electors of Ottawa West, a riding which has been represented by Sir John A. Macdonald and by Sir Robert Borden, to mention only two of the distinguished statesmen who have represented this riding and who have reverenced the House of Commons. I want to thank the people of Ottawa West for sending me here to represent them. I am proud and deeply grateful for this high honour. I will strive to serve them, all of them, in the fullest way.
I wish to pay tribute to the greatest House of Commons man of this generation, and a close personal friend, the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. It is not my intention to deliver another eulogy to Mr. Diefenbaker. The Prime Minister already did that beautifully at the graveside in Saskatoon.
When Mr. Diefenbaker made his maiden speech in this House in 1940, we were suffering the very darkest days of the war. What was it that we were fighting for in that war? What was it that so many Canadians laid down their lives for? What is it that has brought so many people to our shores since the war? If we can answer these questions it may help us with the problems we have in dealing with the future course of this country.
Surely the war was fought, great sacrifices made and millions of new people came to live in Canada because our Canadianism is thought to be worth living for, as so many proved that it was worth dying for.
All the people who have come to Canada have come to build, not to destroy. They have come to practice tolerance and not prejudice. We do not have to undo 500 or 1,000 years of injustice here, but in saying this, Mr. Speaker, we will be wise to give deep thought to our essential Canadianism. It was one of Mr. Diefenbaker's greatest gifts that when he spoke about Canadians, they felt two feet taller. There is still room for builders in Canada notwithstanding perplexing problems both domestic and international. There is still room for growth. I disagree with those who say we can no longer grow in Canada.
I believe the reason this party was elected to form the government is that most Canadians still believe this.
There is a danger of taking our country for granted. The government should constantly remind Canadians about their Canadianism. There should be statues here on Parliament Hill of Canadians who have contributed to the glories of Canada, as there should be statues and reminders elsewhere. I would like to see monuments erected near these buildings to C. D. Howe, J. S. Woodsworth, and some of our prime ministers not now honoured, to other Canadians not only in politics but in all fields of endeavour.
We often talk about putting Canadian content into the CBC. We are concerned about the difficulties faced by

October 15, 1979

Canadian writers and artists. It is time to put Canadian content everywhere in this country. Recently, an American teacher visited Kingston. She was a professor of French and Canadian studies in Cleveland and was attending a seminar in the Kingston area this past summer. She was well equipped with the usual tourist brochures when she went hunting for Sir John A. Macdonald's resting place, among other attractions. She said she found the Hockey Hall of Fame and the Steam Museum in five minutes, but it took her nearly Vh hours looking at gravestones to find Sir John's in Cataraqui cemetery, and she only found it by stumbling across it. This American citizen left $10 to help with the upkeep of the grave. She said if the grave of an equally important national figure was located across Lake Ontario on the American side, it would probably be under an eleven-storey monument.
in coming to this House of Commons for the first time, I considered making some remarks about what has happened to the public service and to the city of Ottawa over the past decade by reason of policies which I consider to be wrong, and also to discuss some of the positive steps that I believe should be taken to diversify the national capital area and improve its economic prospects. But I have decided that I will make these statements in this House on another appropriate occasion.
I do want to speak about a matter which arose during and since the election. I refer to the refugee problem. The refugees have been described as boat people. Apart from aboriginal Canadians, there is a sense in which all Canadians throughout the course of our history have been boat people. We are all descended from boat people; in fact, the first boat people here were with Cartier when he sailed up the St. Lawrence.
I am proud to represent so many people in Ottawa who opened not only their hearts but also their pocketbooks to the boat people. In doing so, they have responded to one of the oldest traditions in Canada, that of helping those from other lands to find a new life with us. 1 would hope the government would be able to devise ways and means of coping with the international refugee problem in some permanent way, because I fear that other dictatorships in the South Pacific and elsewhere may use the same means to get rid of dissenters.
Many of our statesmen, artists and writers have attempted to define what it means to be Canadian. Sir Wilfrid Laurier expressed this Canadian identity as follows:

As for me, I do not want French Canadians dominating anybody and I do not want anybody to dominate them. Equal justice, equal rights. It has been written that the grains of sand of the seas have been counted, that not one hair may fall from our head without the intervention of an eternal and wise Providence. Isn't there reason to believe that, when the supreme battle was waged on the Plains of Abraham and we lost. Providence had intended the two races heretofore enemies to live in peace and harmony from then on upon this continent forming a single nation? There-
-said Sir Wilfrid Laurier-
-lies the idea which presided over the creation of Confederation. When the British provinces were united under the same constitution, the then openly admitted hope was to give to all its scattered components the same national ideal, offering the world the image of a nation diverse in its origins upholding
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
among all its elements the respect for family traditions and ethnic pride, but hereafter providing to all a single and common aspiration.

Mr. Speaker, the people living in this country today should be, I repeat, the envy of all. They have better opportunities for full and rewarding lives, more so than ever before, and very few places in the world can match these opportunities. But I say to you, sir, that it will be our responsibility to ensure that Canada and Canadians remain the envy of all.
1 look forward to being a part of this new government which the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) said here this morning is a government with a mandate for change. 1 look forward to working under the dynamic leadership of the Prime Minister and his cabinet. We have all inherited a rich endowment of wisdom and nature. May we never forget it. Let us Conservatives remember, as Lord Hailsham so wisely pointed out, that we are not curators of a museum, but cultivators of a garden. [Translation]
In those words, Mr. Speaker, 1 say: Evil be to him who evil thinks.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Binks), who has just delivered his maiden speech, I should like to congratulate him not only on his election to the House of Commons but on his spirited first appearance in this chamber. At the same time, I should like to congratulate the Speaker on his re-election as Speaker of the House, a re-election which was based upon his performance in the last Parliament, one which was such that his selection was the unanimous choice of this chamber.
The mover (Mr. Fretz) and the seconder (Mr. MacDonald (Cardigan)) of the address performed extremely well and I congratulate them, too. Of course, I congratulate all the new members who have been elected to this chamber, as well as the older members who have survived the election and who once again appear here, as a large number of us do.

October 15, 1979
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
However, it is not an encouraging period for re-elected members on the other side of the House. It seems that in the selection of his cabinet, the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has placed very low priority on service in the House of Commons and a very low priority on a distinguished record in this chamber. How, otherwise, could one explain the exclusion from the cabinet of such persons as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin)-unfortunately, he is not in the House today-the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), and a whole list of members on the other side who, had they been added to the cabinet, would have performed much more capably than those we have witnessed falter through the question period demonstrating their lack of grasp of our procedures?
All of us have come through an election which was conducted under the electoral reforms approved in the last Parliament. Basing my judgment on my experience, the general framework of these reforms, especially the norms applied to spending, collection and assistance from the public treasury in the running of the election, proved to be sound, although there may be changes which ought to be implemented, and added a much needed reform to our electoral system. We on this side welcome the indication made by the Prime Minister, first in the Speech from the Throne and later in his address, that the procedures of the House of Commons are to be examined in the Committee on Procedure and Organization. We on this side will participate constructively in that re-examination and strive to improve the operation of the House where that is possible.
We need, of course, the fresh views brought into the House by new members who sit in this Parliament in all quarters, and I hope the process adopted in the effort to improve our rules will be such that the contribution of new members will be heard and that they will have an opportunity to give expression to fresh and independent opinions after some experience in observing the operations of the House.
1 listened with great interest to the Prime Minister's comments on Parliament. Listening to him, one would almost think that this was the first Parliament of Canada rather than the thirty-first. One got the impression that the world had begun the moment he assumed office. That is not the case, of course. We have a lot of experience in the House of Commons and not all of its operations are bad. I believe we ought not to leave the impression that everything we do is wrong, though there is obviously room for improvement.
The Prime Minister referred to what he called the historic role of Parliament to control the public purse, and went on to say that this role had been eroded by guillotine rules which meant that each year millions of dollars in public spending went unscrutinized and unchallenged. Mr. Speaker, that statement is certainly an indictment of the official opposition, now the government, while they were sitting on this side of the House. "Unscrutinized and unchallenged", the Prime Minister says about spending proposals. We shall show the country, if he was not able to show the country, how that scrutiny can take place under this particular opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
I will go further and remind the right hon. gentleman that when he talks about the erosion of Parliament, it is an erosion, if that be the case, in which members of the Conservative party participated fully. I say this because I have before me copies of the Journals which show that in 1968 our current rules were adopted unanimously by every member of the House including the Prime Minister's party, led then by the gentleman who is now promoting a new policy for the Prime Minister in the Middle East. So, if there are complaints about the current procedure, let the government take its responsibility for the role members of the Conservative party played in implanting it upon the House of Commons. I shall have more to say about that later, Mr. Speaker.
Of course, the media, especially, are obsessed with the possible length of this Parliament. I am often asked how long the Thirty-first Parliament is going to last. I say that it does not depend mainly upon the opposition; it depends mainly upon the government. It depends on how well and how skilfully the government manages the affairs of this House, how sensitively it reacts to the moods of the House of Commons and how carefully it assesses public opinion in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We are in for four years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
If it is able to do these things, its prospects for existence are much greater than if the conduct exhibited so far by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) becomes the model for members of the government.
We have before us now a very important issue which will permit the government to show the qualities it wants to bring to bear upon the operation of the business of this House, and that is the matter of Petro-Canada. Here it has an opportunity to demonstrate whether it is willing to conciliate or whether it wishes to facilitate, by its stubborn insistence on an ideological position, its own demise.
We have had a list of bills put forward by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker), and it is interesting to look at it because obviously it is the first result of the long summer. It is a very lengthy list of bills, about 90 in all. We have succeeded, in past sessions, in passing about 40 to 60 bills, and I wonder how this enormous amount of business is to get through the House unless the government proposes to impose upon the House an even more severe form of guillotine to which the Prime Minister took exception in his speech.
The list is lengthy, but unimpressive. It is mainly concerned with administrative matters and is very weak on policy-oriented bills. In fact, many of the bills are drawn from the leftovers or holdovers from the last Parliament of Canada. There are very important omissions. There is no bill on the referendum, which is a remarkable omission. There is no bill on the international economic boycott. Remember the vigour and passion with which hon. members now sitting on the government side demanded that we proceed with a bill dealing with
October 15, 1979

the international economic boycott? There is no mention of it in the list.
There is no mention of a bill on public service staff relations but, of course, there are such urgent matters as income tax international conventions, Montreal and Quebec port wardens, a Canada-France champagne agreement, a migratory birds convention and matters relating to caribou migration. If the Prime Minister was serious about getting 90 bills through the House of Commons, why did he not call Parliament much earlier?

speechtext:
Why was Parliament not called? Why have we witnessed the longest adjournment or absence of Parliament probably in the history of Canada or, certainly, in its modern history? This government has taken a very leisurely approach.
Early this year hon. members opposite were clamouring for a budget. They were asking the former minister of finance to bring in another budget following the budget he had brought in in November. Today is October 15, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) has not bestirred himself yet to bring in a budget and we have not been told when that budget will be brought in, except that it will be brought in before Christmas.
There has been absolutely no urgency exhibited by this government in calling Parliament or preparing a legislative program for this House of Commons. Having said that, I want to add a further comment. In the light of that record it ill behooves the government to put pressure on the House of Commons to move quickly. If time were needed and if matters were urgent, then it was open to members of the government to call the House, to have at the present time brought forward its bills and to have had behind them five to eight weeks of legislative work.
We know what the immediate agenda is to be. We have to complete this debate. We have to deal with the budget bills which were uncompleted in the last session. They now become the budget bills of the new government. It will not be the former minister who will move these bills and recommend them to the House; it will be the new Minister of Finance, seconded by a member of this government. This government must get through budget bills. That is a big second item. Maybe, as has been the case in the past, the bringing on of these bills will initiate a very important economic debate. Who knows?
Then we have the spending program of the new government put before the House last Thursday by the President of the Treasury Board. Then we have the first budget, hopefully before Christmas, of the new Minister of Finance. After having dealt with all of these matters, how much more can we do? Maybe the freedom of information bill before Christmas or in the early part of the session, maybe conflict of interest legislation, but let me say that working very hard, in the light of the delay the government has imposed upon this House, it will be very difficult to stack up an impressive list of legislative achievements in the early part of the session.
The Address-Mr. MacEachen
I want to make reference to the spending program, the main estimates and the supplementary estimates tabled by the President of the Treasury Board. These estimates were tabled unchanged from those which were tabled by the former president of the treasury board. Remember, when they were tabled by the former president, the words of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) to the House of Commons in commentary on those estimates? They were "cooked". They were "deceptive". They were "dishonest". We were "concealing things". Lo and behold, despite these strictures, after 4'A months in government the same estimates are brought forward by the new government. Hon. members opposite had plenty of time if they wished to alter those estimates.

October 15, 1979
The Address-Mr. MacEachen will not take responsibility. I just leave that thought with the President of the Treasury Board with the expectation that upon reflection he will take a more co-operative attitude with the House of Commons as he asks us to vote more than $50 billion for the purposes of the government without being prepared to say to the House that he really wants them and takes responsibility for the amounts of money that are requested. I leave that subject there because it is a matter to which we can return later.
Now I want to say a word about the structure of the cabinet and particularly the fact that the representative of the province of Nova Scotia in the Government of Canada is excluded from the main decision-making body of this country. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacKay) is not a member of the inner cabinet; he is not a member of the main decision-making body of this country. 1 want to tell the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) that that situation is unacceptable to the province of Nova Scotia, and 1 ask the Prime Minister to restore to Nova Scotia the position in the Government of Canada that it has occupied since confederation.
In my lifetime seats have been occupied in the cabinet by such people as the late J. L. Ilsley, the late Robert Winters and the late George C. Nowlan, and I wonder whether either one of them would have accepted the situation of being left cooling his heels in Ottawa or some other part of Canada while the big boys were in Jasper making the important decisions. That is the question that is agitating the interests of the people in my province and, I am sure, the people who have supported the Progressive Conservative candidates in Nova Scotia in the last election. Why is it that our minister is not in the inner cabinet? Why is it indeed that Newfoundland with seven members in the House of Commons deserves two ministers, one of whom sits in the inner cabinet, and Nova Scotia with 11 members deserves only one minister who is not entitled to sit with the big boys when they make the decisions? I am not complaining about the generous treatment given to Newfoundland, but I am asking that equally generous treatment be given to the historic province of Nova Scotia.

The Speech from the Throne talks about strengthening the mandate of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Well, that is idle talk. The way to strengthen the mandate of that important department is to put the minister in the inner cabinet. The fact that the government, so it is said, has placed such high priority on questions of regional economic expansion and yet has excluded from the decision-making body the Minister of DREE defies description. I ask the government to bring forward their bill which is intended to strengthen the mandate of regional economic expansion and we will use that occasion to urge the government to make the first start in strengthening the department by putting its minister where he ought to be.
I know a little something about representing a small province in the cabinet of Canada and I am telling you, Mr. Speaker, that it is tough enough to represent a small province

and achieve its objectives in the cabinet when you are present; it is quite impossible when you are absent. I could go on and cite instances, in my opinion, of inaction, wrong actions or inordinate delays affecting the province of Nova Scotia, which I attribute to the absence of the minister from the main decision-making body of the cabinet. I will return to that subject later as I want to say just a word or two about an incident that happened during the question period last Friday when we were talking about the policy of the Government of Canada on the Middle East.
The unsureness of this government has been demonstrated time and time again by confusion and uncertainty, and that is especially true in the field of foreign policy. Confusion and uncertainty are the order of the day. It was added to, heightened and strengthened last Friday when we put questions to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) asking them to tell us what their current policy is on the moving of the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem.
The day after he was sworn in as Prime Minister the leader of the government said, referring to the question of the embassy, that "these questions are now beyond discussion as to their appropriateness". He said that these questions are now beyond discussion, but on Friday neither the Prime Minister nor the Secretary of State for External Affairs would tell us what their current policy is. Is it still the intention of the government to move the embassy? You can imagine the confusion that existed in our embassies throughout the world when the message went out on the weekend telling them what their minister and their Prime Minister said. What would they say to an inquirer on Monday when asked what the government is now thinking about the matter of the embassy and the recognition of Jerusalem as the capital of Israel? In one answer the Prime Minister not only cast doubt upon the status of the decision to move the embassy, he cast doubt upon the policy of the government toward the Palestinian Liberation Organization and, thirdly, he cast doubt on Mr. Stanfield as an ambassador. It requires a master of uncertainty to achieve those three objectives in one single answer.

Since I do not want to take advantage of the latitude of the House, I would like to conclude by mentioning two particular matters. The first matter has to do with the question, asked by the minister. She asked the question, "What is Canada doing in certain parts of the world?" The press informs us that the original text said, "What is Canada doing in Africa?", but I am not quarrelling about that. She may have wanted to blunt the strength of her policy or her suggestion by saying, "What is Canada doing in certain parts of the world?"
Indeed, what is Canada doing in certain parts of the world? What is Canada doing in Africa? Canada is in Africa because in Africa live among the poorest people of the world. What is Canada doing in Asia? What is Canada doing in South America? What is Canada doing in the Caribbean? The minister said that we are not there because of trade, and because we do not have trade we are not there because we are a colonial empire. That is true.
Does the minister not realize that we are there because basically we believe in a humanitarian approach to the solutions of the world's problems, that we believe that peace and stability in the world cannot be achieved unless we alleviate misery and poverty, unless we give full human rights to these people? Why is the minister uncertain? Why is she casting

October 15, 1979
The Address-Mr. MacEachen doubt on the fact that Canada is directing large parts of its aid to the poorest countries of the world? I hope that she will take a very early opportunity to clarify this question because there is great concern in this country and elsewhere that Canada is receding from its commitment to these poorest of the poor.
I could go on and quote statements made by the Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition or statements made by the parliamentary secretary to the minister which contradict totally the new posture which the minister has given to international development questions. 1 can tell her right now that we disagree on that question. I think 1 am making history today, Mr. Speaker, as a native son from western Canada reminding this House of Commons that Canada today has its first western born Prime Minister. There have been other prime ministers from other provinces, such as Bennett from New Brunswick and Diefenbaker from Ontario, who lived most of their youth and mature lives in western Canada, but we have today reached maturity in confederation with the first Prime Minister born and raised in western Canada, in the historic centre of High River.

October 15, 1979

1 should like to remind the House leader for the official opposition of the words used by his leader in his speech the other day. I know the rules about quoting from Hansard, Mr. Speaker, but there are only a few lines and 1 hope members as distinguished as those across the floor from me and who are very experienced will excuse me for quoting from a speech in the same debate. The right hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) said, as reported at page 30 of Hansard:
I should like now to touch upon the manner in which, as members of the Liberal party, we intend to play the important role of representatives of the official opposition. There is no doubt that the people of Canada have given the Progressive Conservative party a mandate to govern Canada and want us to give them the chance to administer our country without being exposed to political interference and chicanery. Not only do we accept and respect the decision of the people, but we will take seriously the responsibility with which we have been entrusted to co-operate constructively in the preparation of Canadian policies.
To me that means the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, at that moment of truth, informed the House that he and his party intend to give the government a chance to govern. For this I congratulate him.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to turn to the subject of my speech today which is confined to one issue and one issue alone. The debate in reference to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne gives every member the opportunity of expressing their views on a crusade which they have been waging and, in addition, gives them an opportunity to set out grievances and recommendations to remedy the crusade as it affects the nation and the constituency.
For ten long years 1 have been pressing the Canadian government-now it will be governments-and various ministers of the day, namely, the secretary of state for external affairs, the solicitor general and the minister of justice, for some action regarding the treatment that young Canadians have received when arrested in Mexico.
At the outset, let me say that no matter how evil the conduct of a human being, or how low he sinks in society, no matter how degrading that conduct may be in reference to the standards set by society, such person is entitled to be treated with dignity as a human being, to the full protection of the law and, indeed, kindness, charity and understanding. They should receive punishment only after due process of law. While awaiting trial such persons should always be regarded as innocent because of the presumption of innocence under our system.
Like many others in this House, 1 have spent my lifetime trying to assist people who have run afoul of the law so as to assure that the rule of law as we know it, whether applied in Canada or elsewhere, should govern the conduct of the process of law rather than have people governed by the rule of people. People who are arrested legally, and sometimes illegally, need head and heart concern. Those who have had the privilege of being moulded in a good environment-an environment of the home, the school, society and other institutions-do not often suffer the horrendous trauma of law enforcement. This can be due to their appreciation of responsibility to society or because they are entitled to the best counsel. That is not to suggest for one moment that those who have enjoyed those privileges do
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
not at times flaunt society's rules and regulations; the law should be applied equally to all.
On October 12 last, 1 put the following question in this House:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I join with others who genuinely offer her good wishes.
My question arises from the fact that Kirk Thomas and Mark Rollin were arrested in Mexico last June and held in jail for three months without charge under circumstances which John Howard, the prison reformer of the eighteenth century, would have found deplorable and inhumane even in England at that time.
My question was very simple: Would the minister make a protest? Had I been permitted-and I am not going to say anything about that at the moment although I may later-to ask one further short question, my point would have been made clear. 1 should like to put on the record the question I would have asked at that time. 1 would have asked the minister if she would further protest that dozens of Canadian families in Canada are being ripped off to the tune of thousands of dollars, and in this particular case $10,000, to get the youths home from Mexican jails. On the face of it, in many cases there would appear to be a fraudulent conspiracy-and I do not say this lightly-among Mexican officials who obtained this money for the release of these young people through our embassy, through action which is not acceptable by our standards. In this particular case the youths were held for three months without charge.
In brief, this is one of a dozen examples I have raised in this House and others that have not been mentioned. Kurt Thomas and Mark Rollin, aged 19 and 20 respectively, of Sherwood Park, Edmonton, Alberta, were arrested in Mexico on June 30 last because they went joy riding in a boat in Mexico without the consent of the owner. 1 do not defend their actions. Even in this country that would be illegal. 1 am, however, condemning what occurred following their arrest, which was a duplication of what happened in many cases with Canadian citizens visiting Mexico as tourists. In Canada this offence would just result in a summary conviction.
They were arrested on June 30 and held in a jail at La Paz for three months without charge, without medical attention, without dental attention and in the most filthy cell, and were forced to eat out of a dish that no respectable Canadian or citizen of the western world would consider suitable.
The parents, Mr. and Mrs. Gerd Thomas, made one or two trips to Mexico and at first put up $4,697.67 payable, as 1 understand it, to our embassy for lawyers' fees and restitution for a boat which was not damaged and was returned. In addition and inclusive of that amount of money, they paid out almost $10,000 for one expense or another, most of which under our system or that of any civilized nation would be unnecessary. It would be neither condoned by the law societies of Canada nor by the law of Canada.
After some time in jail the Thomases were allowed to see their son. He had not had a bath for many months; his hair was down past his shoulders; he was unwashed, unkempt and

October 15, 1979
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
unclean. Elis parents brought pressure to bear on everyone they felt had some authority to do something. Finally, after paying the sum of approximately $10,000 for expenses of one kind or another, their son and his friend were released. Charges were withdrawn which had been laid only during the last part of the three months in order to make legal what was illegal.
1 might add that I have raised my voice before in reference to matters of this kind. To come to the point, when young people are arrested in Mexico-1 have ample evidence, not only from reading the report of the special subcommittee of the Senate of the United States but also from facts concerning other cases in Canada where the incarceration of Canadian and American youth takes place in Mexico-a method is followed. This method, and I have no hesitation or reservation in saying this, is to extort money from parents to the total of their bankroll. Many of these people are hardworking folk, perhaps earning small salaries. After something like this occurs, these people are left bankrupt or in debt.
Let me mention another case in passing which took place on October 22, 1976. This case was reported in The Globe and Mail. I quote from this article:
Jane and Ray Bethune have been trying since January to free their daughter from jail.
Longshoreman Ray Bethune, 56, says he has spent $18,000, wiped out his savings and taken out a bank loan during the past eight months trying to get his 22-year-old daughter out of a Mexican jail.
He says that Canadian government officials told him to keep quiet or his daughter Sharon would suffer at the hands of the Mexicans.
I might pause there. If hon. members look at a report of the special subcommittee of the United States Senate, they will see page after page of evidence which shows that what I have said is correct and that what was written almost three years ago in The Globe and Mail is accurate. Mr. Bethune in his interview with The Globe and Mail reporter went on to say:
We just don't know what the hell to do any more-it's been a nightmare.
You have to remember that in Mexico you are guilty until proven innocent; that is where the slowness in the system comes.
Mr. Bethune said his daughter had nothing to do with the alleged crime and her boyfriend had testified to that.
As a result, Mr. Bethune's daughter was finally released. I can read more about that case but it only illustrates the point I am making, which is that none of us endorses Canadian people going to foreign countries and breaking laws. On the other hand, none of us endorses-whatever the facts are in reference to these cases I have outlined and dozens of others-a neighbouring state permitting the extortion of money from innocent parents because of love and affection for their offspring which drain savings and borrowing power just to get a release from these horror jails and holes.
On March 2, 1977-and in this respect I congratulate the previous government which I kept pressing with questions-a treaty was signed among Mexico, Canada and the United States in reference to the exchange of prisoners. The bill I pressed for and the treaties flowing from the bill were to serve as a prototype for Canada in negotiating similar treaties with other countries. The United States and our own government
[Mr. Woolliams.)
accomplished an exchange of prisoners following conviction and sentence; that is to say, after a certain time, the exchange would take place. Mexico bypasses this agreement. The question is why. Canadians are held in jail without charge, without a court appearance and therefore without any process of law that would put the agreement into effect so that the international legal exchange can be properly made. This issue has been raised by me on many occasions.
With respect to the Thomas case, after the parents' visitation, the two accused held in jail for three months, they were finally charged to legalize the illegal and the charges were withdrawn. After much frustration and after the Thomases had borrowed money from the bank, their release did take place.
I have a letter from a former solicitor general, the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox), now a member of the opposition, dated March 28, 1977. In this letter he states:
I must remind you that such a treaty would not include people awaiting trial but only those under sentence or on probation. Those awaiting trial will still have to request assistance from the Canadian embassy which has been quite efficient in certain cases.
Was he right? The agreement was there. However, on April 10, 1978 Mr. Don Jamieson, the former minister of external affairs, pointed out the act would be proclaimed and the treaty for exchange of prisoners approved as a result of negotiations carried out by the government, and indeed as a result of the position others in Parliament had taken. All have protested but without effect. The United States protested. 1 say to the House, read the report of the special committee of the U.S. Senate.
Canada has protested this. In answer to questions I put to former ministers of external affairs they told me they had protested and they did protest. Our present minister has protested, but the illegal process goes on. However, it is the extortion that 1 object to most. Let us bring it to an end. Let us agree that this treaty does not help much, because no charges are laid, no counsel is permitted, no communication is allowed and no accounting of property seized is given. In reading the Senate report I see it says airplanes and automobiles have been taken. These items just disappear. In many cases no reputable attorneys are at hand. In this particular case, $4,600 or more was paid in lawyer's fees which the Thomases say did nothing.
I hear my hon. friend say it is not according to Canadian standards. I say this to the hon. member, that if a lawyer charges a fee and does not act, or he acted in this fashion, under the rules of the law societies of Canada and the law of Canada he would be disbarred. I say to members that if they have constituencies with rotten lawyers, that is their problem and not mine.
Surely it is not too strong to suggest that there is abusive arrest, abuse of the process of law, abuse by extortion, abuse and confiscation of property without compensation, and abuse of what the United Nations has suggested. The testimony given before the special committee of the United States dealing with the same abuse that Canadians have been subjected
October 15, 1979

to-and this is the Senate's finding, not mine-includes, first, physical torture. There is clear evidence of physical torture on the prisoners, such as broken ribs, or electronic shock devices attached to various parts of the prisoners. Second, there is extortion. In this case huge amounts of money were required by lawyers and prison authorities in order to give prisoners bare necessities; amounts average $10,000. Third, there is Mexican inmate involvement. Mexican prisons appear to be run by other prisoners who share in the "take" from American and Canadian prisoners. These people are again in league with local lawyers, prison officials and the police.
The Senate committee finds in some cases that there are conspiracies. There must be a conspiracy for this kind of thing to occur. The requirements are whatever local authorities say they are. Two years is almost standard for investigation purposes.
When one criticizes, one must make some recommendations.
I ask what shall we do? A very careful report should be prepared and sent to the proper department in the United Nations dealing with civil liberties and human rights, pointing out that we and other members of the United Nations protest any further abuse in this regard. The United States has done that. Is that too much to ask?
Second, a study should be made in Canada, instead of our always relying on studies done in the United States. Our study could be similar to that of the United States Senate. This job could be taken on by our Senate or possibly by justice and legal affairs. Witnesses could be subject to the terms and conditions I have pointed out this afternoon in this House. In their evidence they could describe how they have suffered under these conditions and how they were dehumanized. Above all, they could describe what money has been extorted from their parents.
Third, the strongest protest possible should be made by our Department of External Affairs through proper diplomatic channels. As the American subcommittee recommended, a list of reputable lawyers should be kept by our embassy in Mexico. This should be done in light of evidence that came out before the United States subcommittee that lawyers were receiving payments without acting. I already referred to the Thomases where $4,600 was paid to lawyers who did not do anything until the parents went there and visited.
I want to read from these letters. Again I have the letter dated March 28 from the former solicitor general, the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes. I will not read all of it. He emphasized, and I quote:
1 must remind you that such a treaty would not include people awaiting trial-
I pause there. Why are they sometimes held three months, six months or a year until the last dollar is drained from the parents? That is really what the solicitor general was saying in very diplomatic language. He continued:
-those awaiting trial will still have to request assistance from the Canadian embassy-
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
It is time for the Canadian embassy to do as the Americans have done, namely have part of their staff trained in legal matters to understand and comprehend after study the jurisprudence of Mexico in order that they can assist those who get into this plight.
On April 10, 1978 I received a letter from Don Jamieson pointing out that the treaty had been signed. Bill C-21 to which our party, the NDP and all members of the House gave their approval regarding the exchange of prisoners is now being bypassed. This has not been an easy fight; it has been going on for a long time. I wish to read some of the findings of the committee in the United States. I quote:
Similarly, it is difficult to verify complaints of confiscation of personal property when receipts have not been given, or of confirming extortion by an attorney in the absence of a written contract or agreement. Despite the fact that the evidence or lack thereof in this category is "inconclusive", it should be noted the panel believes that these complaints and allegations have some merit since they form a credible pattern. This conclusion is reached even though another pattern similarly emerged from this review indicating that a large number of complaints resulted from self-serving efforts by the prisoners-
In spite of that, they found evidence to the effect that those facts were correct. After summarizing the evidence, the committee said this:
Most of the substantiated cases of denial of access have been protested. Some have been protested formally, by note, to the Mexican government. Other cases, usually outside Mexico City, have been protested to local authorities. Those cases which were not protested represent either an unwillingness on the part of the prisoner to have his name included in a note of protest-often for fear that this might jeopardize his case ... In some jurisdictions there has been noticeable improvement in the notification process; in others, there has been little or no improvement. This is clearly an area in which efforts must continuously be made.
The Senate committee further stated:
Corrective Action Taken: Substantiated findings refer to instances of infrequent visitation by consular officers which occurred mainly between early 1974 and February 1975. During this period the posts were hampered by insufficient funds to permit travel to outlying jails. It is noted, however, that some of the valid complaints in this category were also made by prisoners who were incarcerated in jails nearby, which indicates that visits were irregular and infrequent. Since February 1975 all American prisoners in Mexico who so desired have been visited on a regular basis-
I hope that would be a finding of any one of our committees.
Corrective Action Taken: No action has been taken nor does any action appear to be feasible, since determination of guilt or innocence is a proper function of the Mexican legal system. While a number of cases reflect a vigorous dispute as to the verdict and the manner in which evidence was secured to determine it, the Mexican legal system does provide a forum for the resolution of such disputes.
Therefore they remain in jail without charge.
Substantiated instances of abuse at the time of arrest were protested orally and by note to the Mexican government and/or the local jurisdictional authorities when the prisoner indicated he desired to have a protest made. In many cases the prisoner believed it to be in his best interest not to register a protest, although he did inform the visiting consular officer that he had been subjected to mistreatment.
I am reading this evidence to show how necessary it is for our committee to study this and maybe to set up a similar special committee of cur Senate.
In several cases the embassy or the various consulates in Mexico have been successful in obtaining a return, or at least a partial return, of confiscated personal property.

October 15, 1979
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
They go on to say that personal property disappears because they issue no receipts, as is the case in jails in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. These people have no protection whatsoever.
Although a few of the substantiated cases occurred elsewhere, these would appear to be somewhat isolated incidents rather than the general pattern of prison life.
It goes on to point out that where there is a local authority, prisoners are better treated. However, in a city like Mexico City where the jurisdiction is of wider scope, this treatment is still continuing.
In a majority of cases, however, the prisoner chooses not to have a protest made in his behalf. This may be from fear of reprisal from the "mayores" or their "commandos", or from fear of being transferred to another cell block and thereby losing many of the privileges the prisoner has already paid for.
These are findings of a committee that studied this situation.

Mr. Speaker, this is an historical moment in my life, naturally. It is the first time I have had the privilege to speak in this chamber. In a way I feel partly at home because of the general ecclesiastical look of the place and from the fact that the traditional place of holding Parliament was an old abbey. In my nomination speech and all through the campaign that I carried out for many months I stated in that first speech, and many times afterward, that it was my intention to defend human life from its conception until its natural end. In doing so I tried to lay down quite simply the fact of my basic belief in human rights which has been expressed by many members of this House already in this session. My basic belief is that each human being has been given the right to life and that this right continues until they naturally die. These rights are sometimes of an individual nature and sometimes of a collective nature. They ought not to be infringed upon at any time.
Now, both in our country and in the world infringement of human rights continues. During that short space of time that we human beings have to live on this planet, you and I, Mr. Speaker, and all others have somehow or other to struggle and fight to see that the rights of all human beings are safeguarded, and one of the rights that I consider to be basic to each of us is the right to health. That right encompasses and takes into account all the other human living conditions that are necessary to make it possible for a person to live as a healthy person. And when 1 speak of health I speak not only of the physical health which we all hope to have, but also of the psychological, moral, spiritual and emotional health which makes it possible for a human being to live as a human being and, more important, makes it possible for a nation to live as a healthy nation and the world to live as a healthy community of nations. So when I speak of health, I do not speak merely of the medical state which so frequently is used as the whole standard; 1 speak of the whole integrated reality that makes up the well-being of all people.
As 1 have said, it is one of my basic personal convictions that the right to health is one of the most important rights we have as human beings, and that if we as Canadian citizens want really to make a mark at the United Nations it is important that we show the way with a model of ourselves rather than with a pointing of the finger at others who have so far not reached that level of health.
It was basically because of this that 1 was disappointed in the Speech from the Throne. 1 found quite quickly that there was not a single mention of health or the social principles and bases which are needed to bring about a healthy society. The question of health and more specifically the question of medical care have in no way been totally settled in this country. A
The Address-Mr. Ogle
former member of Parliament of my party, Tommy Douglas, said this past weekend in Toronto that he believes that there is a grave danger for our country because the medical care system we now have is under serious pressure and could, in a sense, disintegrate. In the next few minutes I would like to direct some of my remarks to that particular problem and crisis. I agree that it is one of the main problems in our country today.
In passing 1 will say that the right to health is not listed as such among the rights of the United Nations, but in article 25 a much broader stand, what I like to think of as rights across the board, was stated as follows:
Every human being has the right to a standard of living adequate to ensure his health and well-being, as well as those of his family-particularly as regards their need for food, clothing, shelter, and medical care, as well as the necessary social services...
In May, 1977 at the World Health Assembly our country went on record when it adopted the global health goal, which is as follows;
That the main social targets of governments and the World Health Organization in the coming decades should be the attainment by all citizens of the world by the year 2000 of a level of health that will permit them to lead a socially and economically productive life.
I personally feel we should keep that goal before ourselves all the time.
In the coming years there will be many areas of health about which I would like to speak. One of them will be the whole question of human nutrition and food. 1 have lived part of my life in the developing world. I have lived with starving people whose main problem was lack of food, but I think that wc and people like ourselves who live with bounty but who many times are overfed and undernourished must seriously look into the whole question of food as it is used and eaten in our country. We must look critically at artificial foods and ingredients which make "natural" food anything but natural food.
On the question of medicare once more, I have heard various speakers in the past week in this House refer to medicare. Many of them claimed that they had a great deal to do with its founding, but I personally had the experience of living very close to the heart of the medicare crisis of 1962 in Saskatchewan when the first universal medicare plan in North America came into effect. The battle began on July 1 of that year and continued until July 23. There was a basic tearing apart of many people because of the intensity of that head-on struggle, but it finally resulted in a signed declaration in Saskatoon on July 23 which gave the province of Saskatchewan the first medicare plan in North America.
At that time I was younger than I am today, of course, but by a particular accident of fate I was living directly between the two sides. The government of Saskatchewan was headquartered in the Bessborough Hotel, and the medical profession was headquartered in the medical building just a few hundred yards down the street. Directly in the centre of that was the old Catholic Centre of which I used to be the director. During those 23 days I literally lived in no man's land.

I feel now that those 23 days had a great influence on my life in relation to many other social questions. It was an education to be there and to see that finally social change of a basic nature came about only when a group of people had in themselves a vision and, more than a vision, the courage to bring about that vision even though everyone seemed to be against them.

From that beginning in Saskatchewan in 1962 the notion of a medicare scheme spread to other provinces. However, that came after. Because there was a problem of magnitude-medicare would affect everybody-a former prime minister, now deceased, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, made an historic decision and appointed in 1961 Mr. Justice Emmett Hall to study the health needs of Canadians. I believe the resulting report should seriously be looked at again by all Canadians because that document outlines the basics of medicare.
Some of the recommendations in that report have been put into effect, but many have never yet been attempted. There are visions in that document which have not really come to light anywhere as yet, but I invite one and all to look again at that document. In the document there were four basic principles which were necessary to have a medicare scheme function. The first was that there should be comprehensive coverage; everyone should be in the scheme. The second principle was that there should be universal availability; that it would be possible for everybody to receive health care. The third was that there should be portable benefits; one could travel from one place to another and still be taken care of. Finally, it should be administered by a central, non-profit administration. That has worked, more or less, in different places and in different ways, but in the last year or so I feel that obvious cracks have begun to appear in the system. Doctors are now opting out, which has a different wording in different places. There is double billing or something else, which is to say that the system is not being followed. Premiums are now going to be charged in Newfoundland, for instance, which again goes against the very basic nature of the medicare idea.
When things like this begin to happen, we have a dangerous situation on our hands. To draw an analogy, the four principles to which 1 referred could be regarded as something like the legs of a chair. If one leg of a chair was shorter than the others, the chair would be wobbly and a very uncomfortable place to sit. If one began to cut the legs so that a balance could be obtained by giving up a part of one of the legs, the chair really would not become balanced. A more critical situation would develop, finally causing the person sitting on the chair- and I do not know what words I can use in the House-to fall to the floor. That is what will happen with the medicare scheme and plan unless something of a drastic nature is done to stop the erosion that is taking place.

speechtext: Now I should like to quote from the speech which Tommy Douglas gave in Toronto this weekend in which he expressed ideas that are very close to mine. 1 should like to state the ideas of a person for whom I have great respect and who, in total truth, can be called the father of medicare, namely, Mr. Douglas. He said, and it is true, that the majority of doctors across Canada are operating under medicare plans. He said also that if fee schedules are not adequate under provincial plans, then fair schedules should be negotiated between the provinces and the doctors. Another thing that Mr. Douglas said, and which I feel is a very good point, is that if a doctor wants to opt out, then he should be allowed to do so, but he should opt right out and not use the scheme to get part of what he wants and something else to get some more of what he wants. The vast majority of doctors will remain with the scheme and receive an adequate income for their services, but if they opt out, then, I suggest, they should do without the public services which they frequently use under the medical care plan. That is a very serious point and one which I hope this government will take to heart. I hope that the government will ensure that that practice stops under the present legislation.
There are certain areas of health care which I think deserve special attention. I will pass over them quickly. I feel that health care in the whole area of industry is a point to which this government will have to pay special attention. In the area of health care, psychiatric care in the penitentiary system, special notice will have to be taken by the government. Odyssey, a group of inmates at Millhaven working for constructive, non-violent change, produced a working paper in August of this year alleging that medical and psychiatric neglect and abuse are rampant in Canadian penitentiaries. That should be dealt with immediately by the government.
Then there is the whole problem of the Indian native population. A serious injustice is being done to these people because of the appallingly inferior level of health care being provided to the native communities. The average life expectancy is 10 to 20 years less for a native; health and mortality is two to three times as high as the national average; their caloric intake is well below the national average; the number of doctors and nurses caring for them is well below the national average.
In the new charter which Mr. Hall produced the following is stated:
There is clearly an overriding national interest in the health of Canadians wherever they reside. We are a mobile people and illness knows no provincial boundaries nor other differences... What the commission recommends is that... as a nation we now take the necessary legislative, organizational, and

October 15, 1979
financial decisions to make all the fruits of the health sciences available to all our residents without hindrance of any kind. All our recommendations are directed toward this objective.
That paper is 15 years old but it is still extremely relevant.
As 1 only have a few moments left, may I recount a story in summing up and leave with the House something on which to reflect. The story has to do with neighbourliness and who is our neighbour. 1 will tell it as it is oulined in the Gospel according to Saint Luke.
The question of who is my neighbour and how must I care for him is an old one. According to the Gospel, a lawyer asked Jesus one day, in an attempt to justify himself, "And who is my neighbour?". Jesus replied that a man was once on his way down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell into the hands of thieves. They took all he had, beat him and then made off, leaving him half dead. Now, a priest happened to be travelling down the same road, but when he saw the man, he passed by on the other side. In the same way, a Levite who came to the place saw him and passed by on the other side. But a Samaritan traveller who came upon him was moved with compassion when he saw him. He went up and bandaged his wounds, pouring oil and wine on them. He then lifted him on his own mount, carried him to the inn and looked after him. Next day, he took out two denarii and handed them to the innkeeper. "Look after him," he said, "and on my way back I will make good any extra expense you have." Which of these three do you think proved himself a neighbour to the man who fell into the thieves' hands? The lawyer answered, "The one who took pity on him." Jesus said to him, "Go, and do the same yourself."
It is an old story, a new story, the same story about three groups of people involved. The first group consisted of the thieves who came upon this person. Their principle of life was: What is yours is mine. So they took all he had.
An hon. Mlember: That is the NDP all right.
